16331-new-york-times-current-history-the:
This volume of New York Times Current History gathers documents and comment from the European War's first months. A statement approved by Dr. Dernburg, dated November 1, 1914, argues that Austria-Hungary and Russia, whose differences sharpened for years, made the struggle unavoidable after the Sarajevo tragedy. Germany and France, tied by alliances, joined them, while Italy and England, each tied to one side yet removed from the continent, faced uncertain choices.

Current History gave American readers the war in documents, maps, and essays as it unfolded. The volume preserves German, Allied, and neutral voices side by side. Students of the First World War will find a valuable contemporary record of how the war was explained.
23646-the-pharaoh-and-the-priest-an-hist:
Alexander Glovatski's historical novel of ancient Egypt reached English readers in 1902 through Jeremiah Curtin, translator of Quo Vadis and With Fire and Sword. Its setting is the Nile valley, where every acre of rich soil was laid down by river mud from inner Africa, and where grain from Egyptian fields fed Rome, Greece, and Judaea.

That wealth could only be worked by a whole people directed together. The novel's conflict grows from that fact: the pharaoh and the priesthood, the two powers that commanded the land's labor, contend for control of Egypt. Curtin prefaces the tale with an essay on Egypt's unique place, making this both a romance of the ancient world and a study of power built on the river.

new-york-times-current-history-the-europ:
The New York Times issued this number of its Current History magazine on the European War. It covers the start of the war to March 1915. Its theme is set as a question: Who Began the War, and Why? The contents begin with the case for Germany.

Speeches by Kaiser Wilhelm the Second fill much of the number. He forgives enemies, speaks from the throne, and addresses the German army and navy. Other pieces cheer the men as one for the Kaiser, hearts for God and fists on the enemy. His letter to Lord Tweedmouth is also printed. Readers in America could weigh Germany's own words early in the war.
podcast-tuckercarlson-JS-3QssVPeg:
Economist Jeffrey Sachs joins Tucker Carlson to give what the title calls the untold history. It covers the Cold War as he reconstructs it, and the CIA coups that punctuated it around the world. It also covers the origin of Covid. On that subject Sachs has broken publicly with the official account he once helped administer.

Sachs chaired the Lancet's Covid commission and emerged convinced the virus likely came from laboratory work, a position he argues here alongside his longer indictment of American foreign policy. Carlson, an eager host for both arguments, lets him build the full arc. Sachs's views are contested by many former colleagues; his standing makes the contest significant. The episode preserves a pillar of the establishment prosecuting the establishment, in detail, which is a rarer document than any outsider's critique.
